newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong socialites revel at big ball.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong socialites revel at big ball.

text.p: If you want to sell a Swiss watch, put 200 Hong Kong millionaires in a hotel ballroom and turn on the dry ice.

Capitalist Hong Kong may be just 10 days away from a new life under Communist China but conspicuous consumption reigned supreme on Friday night for the last big ball before the British colony is handed over to Beijing.

Rolls-Royces queued outside a luxury hotel to disgorge the beautiful people. Paparazzi jostled to snap the celebrities. Socialites vied with starlets to snatch the limelight. The scent of expensive perfume filled the air.

The chattering classes were out in force for the launch of Philippe Charriol's new collection of Swiss watches and the organisers, who put on a futuristic fashion show swirling in dry ice, said one in two of the 400 guests were millionaires.

In the runup to the handover, Hong Kong's frenetic social scene has been transformed with ex-patriate Britons taking a back seat to the affluent Chinese, bedecked in diamonds and designer dresses as they quaff champagne.
Charriol, sporting a giant red rose in his buttonhole as he swooped to kiss his guests in the marble hallway, exuded charm and proudly boasted: "Everybody is here."
For him, the historic switch had already happened.
"It is a case of 'The King is dead, long live the King.' The handover is a mere formality. People feel good. The Chinese can cope with any situation -- they are fantastic," he said.
But didn't he think there would be a clash of cultures and ideology? "It is pure capitalism over there (in China) but there is a communist framework. The growth in China is absolutely amazing."

In the dying days of empire, the British high society matron is an endangered species. The new queens of the charity ball are the Chinese millionaires' wives, known as tai tai's (Mandarin for Madam or Wife).
Typical of the new breed is Eunice Lam who had just come back from a trip to Beijing. She forecast more of a social mix. "Now many people from the mainland are involved," she said.
"I'm sure the ex-patriates from the UK are going to miss Hong Kong. They don't want to go home. I hope China will accept them as friends," she added.
Fanny Ma, the quintessential tai tai who is married to a property developer and active in charity work, faced the future with equanimity but agreed the handover was an emotional time.
"We have butterflies in the stomach. We are very excited but with mixed emotions," she said.
